notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Genesis 24:46–67, drawn from the sources I was able to reach:

---

## Genesis 24:46–49 — The Servant Finishes His Report to Rebekah’s Family

**v. 46:** The servant recounts how Rebekah “made haste” and repeated her double offer — drink for him and water for the camels. This retelling underscores Rebekah’s character: her willingness and industry are not just one-time acts but consistent traits. The servant wants the family to see that her actions matched the very sign he had prayed for.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

**v. 47:** The servant explains that after asking whose daughter she was and learning she was “the daughter of Bethuel, Nahor’s son, whom Milcah bore,” he placed the nose-ring and bracelets on her. Gill notes that this confirmed she was of Abraham’s own kindred — Nahor being Abraham’s brother — exactly as Abraham had required.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

**v. 48:** The servant “bowed down and worshiped the LORD.” His worship is immediate and personal. He blesses “the LORD, the God of my master Abraham,” acknowledging that God “led me on the right road.” Keil & Delitzsch note that the servant’s gratitude demonstrates that he saw the hand of God — not luck or coincidence — in his success.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/genesis/24.htm

**v. 49:** The servant presses for a decision: “If you will show kindness and faithfulness to my master, tell me; but if not, let me know.” David Guzik observes that the servant understood he was representing his master, not himself — the answer would be given “to my master,” not to him. The servant would not waste time; if the answer was no, he would “go elsewhere” (lit. “turn to the right hand or to the left”).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

---

## Genesis 24:50–53 — The Family Consents and Gifts Are Given

**v. 50:** “Laban and Bethuel answered, ‘This is from the LORD; we have no choice in the matter.’” Guzik observes that the visible providence of God plus the evident wealth of Abraham’s household made the answer clear to Rebekah’s brother and father. The phrase “we cannot speak to you either bad or good” means they cannot oppose what God has evidently done.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

**v. 51:** “Rebekah is here before you. Take her and go, and let her become the wife of your master’s son, just as the LORD has decreed.” The family acknowledges God’s sovereign decree in the matter.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

**v. 52:** The servant again “bowed down to the ground before the LORD.” Keil & Delitzsch note that the servant’s first response after the family’s consent is worship — “he offered thanks to Jehovah with the deepest reverence.” This is the second time the servant worships in this chapter (see v. 26–27 and v. 48), showing a pattern of gratitude.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/genesis/24.htm

**v. 53:** The servant brings out “jewels of silver and gold, and articles of clothing” for Rebekah and “precious gifts” for her brother and mother. Guzik notes these were additional gifts beyond what he had given at the well (v. 22). They were a kind of dowry (mohar), customary in ancient Near Eastern marriage agreements, demonstrating the bridegroom’s ability to provide. JFB adds that jewels of silver and gold with money “form a woman’s dowry among the pastoral tribes.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-24.html

---

## Genesis 24:54–58 — The Servant’s Urgency and Rebekah’s Decision

**v. 54:** The servant and his men eat, drink, and spend the night. The next morning he requests immediate departure: “Send me on my way to my master.” Guzik notes the servant’s focus and urgency — after traveling roughly 900 miles, he stays only one night before wanting to return. Matthew Henry comments that “lingering and loitering no way become a wise and good man who is faithful to his duty.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-66.htm (Henry)

**v. 55:** Rebekah’s brother and mother ask that she remain “ten days or so” — literally “a few days, at least ten.” Lange’s Commentary explains “a circle of days” or “a decade,” meaning an indefinite period that could stretch. Keil notes the family’s natural desire not to part so suddenly with their daughter.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/genesis-24.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/genesis/24.htm

**v. 56:** The servant insists: “Do not delay me, since the LORD has made my journey a success.” He sees divine success as a reason for urgency, not complacency. Guzik comments that the servant “remained focused on his mission.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

**v. 57:** The family responds, “We will call the girl and ask her opinion.” Dr. Constable notes this was customary in Hurrian society, where the bride was consulted before completing marriage arrangements. The brother Laban takes the lead in negotiations, which was also typical.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-24.html

**v. 58:** Rebekah is asked, “Will you go with this man?” She answers simply, “I will go.” Gill notes that the question was about going *immediately*, not about the marriage itself (which was already agreed). He adds, citing Jarchi, that her answer may even imply “of myself, and even if you are not willing” — expressing her determination. Guzik calls her words “worthy words of faith,” showing remarkable willingness to leave everything familiar for a bridegroom she had never seen.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

---

## Genesis 24:59–61 — Departure and Blessing

**v. 59:** “They sent their sister Rebekah on her way, along with her nurse and Abraham’s servant and his men.” The nurse is later identified as Deborah (Genesis 35:8). Lange notes that in noble families the nurse “usually remained a permanent and valued companion of her foster-child.” The text calls Rebekah “their sister” — literally true of Laban; through betrothal she became the equal of her parents.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/genesis-24.html

**v. 60:** The family blesses Rebekah: “Our sister, may you become the mother of thousands upon thousands. May your offspring possess the gates of their enemies.” Keil & Delitzsch note the blessing is “almost verbatim the same as Genesis 22:17” (God’s promise to Abraham after the binding of Isaac) and that “thousands of myriads” is a “hyperbolical expression for an innumerable host of children.” Lange observes the house of Nahor “formed a certain opposition to the heathen” and shared intuitions about Abraham’s descendants. This blessing has been “richly fulfilled” in the growth of Israel.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/genesis/24.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/genesis-24.html

**v. 61:** Rebekah and her servant girls mount the camels and follow the man. The servant “took Rebekah and left.” Guzik comments that one can imagine the conversations on the journey: “She wanted to know all she could about Isaac, whom she loved without ever seeing, and he would be delighted to tell her.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

---

## Genesis 24:62–63 — Isaac in the Field

**v. 62:** “Isaac had just returned from Beer-lahai-roi, for he was living in the Negev.” Beer-lahai-roi (“Well of the Living One Who Sees Me”) was where Hagar encountered the Angel of the LORD (Genesis 16:14). Constable notes this “was a place where God had previously answered prayer,” which “suggests that Isaac may have been praying for God’s will to be done in the choice of his wife.” Barnes similarly comments that it was “a spot calculated to awaken thoughts of an overruling Providence.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-24.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-66.htm (Barnes)

**v. 63:** “Isaac went out to the field to meditate.” The Hebrew verb *lāśûaḥ* is rare and has been variously rendered: “to pray” (Onkelos, Targum, Luther, Keil), “to meditate” (LXX, Vulgate, most English versions), “to lament” (Knobel, Lange, some modern scholars). Ellicott notes the substantive form of the verb appears in Psalm 104:34 for religious meditation and “this sense well agrees with the whole character of the calm, peaceful Isaac.” Barnes says this is “a characteristic of Isaac’s retiring, contemplative mood… Abraham was the active, authoritative father; Isaac was the passive, submissive son.” Matthew Henry adds: “Holy souls love retirement; it will do us good to be often alone, if rightly employed; and we are never less alone than when alone.”

The Cambridge Bible notes that some modern scholars (Knobel, Ewald, Strack, Gunkel) render the word “to wail” or “lament,” which “has the merit of agreeing with the mention of Isaac’s need of being comforted (v. 67).” The Pulpit Commentary reconciles the views by saying Isaac went out “doubtless to do all three” — to think, to pray, and to lament his mother.

From a Reformed perspective, Ligonier notes that Matthew Henry commented “Meditation and prayer ought to be both our business and our delight when we are alone,” and that “we cannot expect God to guide us if we do not meet with Him in prayer like Isaac.”

Desiring God’s David Mathis writes that the Hebrew word for meditation means literally to “chew” on a thought “as an animal chews the cud,” and that Judeo-Christian meditation “aims to fill the mind while engaging and nourishing the inner person” — the opposite of Eastern meditation that empties the mind.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-63.htm (Ellicott, Barnes, Henry, Cambridge, Keil, Poole)
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/isaac-marries-rebekah (via search excerpt)
— https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/meditate-to-move-mountains

---

## Genesis 24:64–65 — Rebekah Meets Isaac

**v. 64:** “Rebekah looked up and saw Isaac, she got down from her camel.” Keil & Delitzsch note the Hebrew verb *nāfal* (lit. “to fall”) “signifies a hasty descent” (cf. 2 Kings 5:21), done “to receive him, according to Oriental custom, in the most respectful manner.” JFB adds: “If Isaac were walking, it would have been most unmannerly for her to have continued seated; an inferior, if riding, always alights in presence of a person of rank, no exception being made for women.” Constable adds that she “dismounted out of respect for her intended husband (cf. Joshua 15:18; 1 Samuel 25:23).”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/genesis/24.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-24.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-24.html

**v. 65:** Rebekah asks who the man is, and the servant says, “It is my master.” She then “took her veil and covered herself.” JFB explains: “The veil is an essential part of female dress. In country places it is often thrown aside, but on the appearance of a stranger, it is drawn over the face… In a bride it was a token of her reverence and subjection to her husband.” Constable adds: “Her self-veiling hinted at her becoming his bride since it was customary to veil the bride in a marriage ceremony. Normally Israelite women did not wear veils (cf. Genesis 12:14; 38:14).” The Geneva Study Bible calls it “a token of humbleness and purity.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-24.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-24.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gsb/genesis/24.htm

---

## Genesis 24:66–67 — Marriage and Comfort

**v. 66:** “The servant told Isaac all that he had done.” Gill explains this means he reported “by what means he found out the person designed for his wife, and got knowledge of her father’s house… and what agreement he had made with the parents and relations of Rebekah to be his wife.” The servant faithfully reports the entire story of God’s providence to Isaac.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

**v. 67:** “Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah and took Rebekah as his wife. And Isaac loved her and was comforted after his mother’s death.” Several points are made by the traditional commentators:

- **Sarah’s tent:** Gill explains that women in those times and places “had separate apartments from their husbands.” Ligonier notes that “going into Sarah’s tent reveals Rebekah as the covenant community’s new matriarch” (Reformed study Bible view). Ellicott adds that “Leah and Rachel had each her own tent (Genesis 31:33).”
- **“He loved her”:** Barnes observes this is “the first mention of the social affections” in Scripture—a notable detail. “It comes in probably because Isaac had not before seen his bride, and now felt his heart drawn toward her.” Gill connects it to Ephesians 5:28: “as a man ought to love his wife, even as his own body.”
- **Comfort after his mother’s death:** Gill, citing Jewish tradition, says Sarah had died about three years earlier (see Genesis 25:20 where Isaac was 40 at marriage; Sarah died at 127 when Isaac was 37). “His sorrow for his mother subsided, and he became cheerful and comfortable.” Matthew Henry comments: “Observe what an affectionate son Isaac was: it was about three years since his mother died, and yet he was not, till now, comforted. See also what an affectionate husband he was to his wife. Dutiful sons promise fair to be affectionate husbands.”
- **Typology:** The Pulpit Commentary (Barnes) notes that the whole scene is “a description of the primeval marriage… a pure and holy relation, reaching back into the realms of innocence, and fit to be the emblem of the humble, confiding, affectionate union between the Lord and his people.” Guzik (charismatic/Pentecostal perspective) sees a typological picture: “Isaac and Rebekah’s coming together — a father desiring a bride for his son, a son accounted as dead and raised from death, and a lovely bride chosen, called, and lavished with gifts — paints a vivid picture of Jesus and His Church.”

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/isaac-marries-rebekah (via search excerpt)
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-66.htm (Barnes, Henry)
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

---

## Notes on Differing Traditions

**Typological Interpretation (Pentecostal/Charismatic and some Reformed):** Enduring Word (David Guzik) devotes significant space to the typology: Abraham = the Father, Isaac = the Son (accounted as dead on Moriah, then symbolically resurrected), the servant (Eliezer) = the Holy Spirit who seeks a bride for the Son, Rebekah = the Church, called out from the world, lavished with gifts, and brought to the Son. This typological reading is common in charismatic and some Reformed preaching. The Pulpit Commentary (Barnes) also sees the marriage as “the emblem of the humble, confiding, affectionate union between the Lord and his people.”

**Reformed:** Ligonier emphasizes the absence of Abraham from the closing scene — though still alive, “Moses passes over him because he is showing that Isaac takes Abraham’s place as patriarch for the next generation of God’s people.” The Reformed reading stresses covenant succession and God’s providence in guiding both the servant and Isaac through prayer.
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/isaac-marries-rebekah

**Lutheran:** Keil & Delitzsch (a standard Lutheran conservative commentary) emphasizes the providential timing and the etymology of the Hebrew, and renders *lāśûaḥ* as “to pray,” following Luther. They stress that “the object of his going to the field to meditate was undoubtedly to lay the question of his marriage before God in solitude.”

**Baptist:** Gill (staunch Baptist, 18th c.) provides meticulous historical and linguistic detail without much typological elaboration. He focuses on the custom, the legal aspects, and cross-references. Spurgeon (also Baptist), quoted by Guzik, emphasizes the servant as a model of Christian service: “Like every true servant of Christ, he put his master’s business before his own ease or comfort.”

**Anglican:** Ellicott (19th c. Anglican bishop) renders “to meditate” and emphasizes that the Hebrew word’s usage in Psalm 104:34 supports the sense of religious meditation fitting Isaac’s “calm, peaceful” character. No distinctly Anglican doctrinal difference noted for this passage.

**Methodist/Wesleyan:** No distinctly Wesleyan reading emerged from the searches for these specific verses. Matthew Henry’s comments (widely used across traditions) heavily influenced Methodist preaching.
